item.title: [New Hampshire] Deep Dive — State Complaints, ESY, and Compensatory Education
item.description:
This deep dive walks through the three dispute tools that meet in one file folder: the state complaint under 34 CFR 300.151 through 300.153 and New Hampshire's Ed 1121 process (who can file, the sixty-day clock, the commissioner's signed decision, the twenty-day reconsideration rule, and the public complaint summaries required by RSA 186-C:5-a); extended school year under 34 CFR 300.106 and New Hampshire's Ed 1110.01 (individual team determination, the regression and recoupment standard, and the factors beyond regression); and compensatory education under the qualitative "but for" standard of Reid v. District of Columbia, 401 F.3d 516 (D.C. Cir. 2005), including the First Circuit's Pihl decision and real New Hampshire complaint orders that required districts to deliver compensatory services. The board also heard 2025-2026 state assessment results (Nashua proficiency 45% ELA, 34% math, 27% science). Two printed agenda items did not happen: the consent agenda was never taken up in the recording, and the five special education policy first readings (ACE, IHBA, IHBA-R1, IHBAA, IHBAB) previewed from the agenda were not given a first reading — no second-reading date was set. The separate 6 PM Facilities Master Plan public hearing that followed drew roughly 80 speakers, overwhelmingly urging the board to close no schools; no vote was taken, and the board deliberates November 16 (whether it votes that night is unconfirmed).
